# **Per-Test Code Coverage Attribution in the JVM: Beyond Naive Sequential Reset**

Determining precise, per-test execution attribution for modified code diffs is a core requirement for building a deterministic, local verdict layer. Answering whether a changed line is covered by exactly one test or multiple overlapping tests (multiplicity, Q1) and identifying whether two tests exercise identical production paths (redundancy, Q2) requires a per-test coverage map. However, the naive approach—executing a global JaCoCo agent and calling reset() before and getExecutionData(true) after each test sequentially—suffers from severe execution overhead (\~309 ms per test, or \~25 minutes for a 5,000-test suite, modeled under analytical assumptions), races during parallel test execution, and corrupts coverage attribution for static initializers and asynchronous worker threads.  
This report evaluates alternatives to naive sequential resets, details the internals of production engines that solve test-to-code mapping, analyzes parallelized in-memory snapshot architectures, and outlines a rigorous validation suite.

## **1\. Alternative Algorithmic Formulations**

### **A1. Multiplicity Estimation vs. Full Attribution**

To answer Q1 ("Is this changed line executed by exactly one test, or by ![][image1] overlapping tests?"), discovering the exact identity of every covering test is not strictly necessary. Instead, the multiplicity value ![][image1] can be estimated using combinatorial and probabilistic constructs embedded directly into class bytecode.

#### **Counting Sketches and Probabilistic Set Membership**

Bytecode instrumentation can allocate a fixed array of counters (a Count-Min sketch) or registers (HyperLogLog) per probe location. During test ![][image2], execution of probe ![][image3] invokes a lightweight static hook passing the current test index ![][image4]. The hook hashes ![][image4] across ![][image5] hash functions and increments the corresponding counter buckets.  
While HyperLogLog (HLL) provides an accurate estimate of cardinality ![][image1] using fixed memory (![][image6] bits per probe), its probabilistic error bounds (typically ![][image7], where ![][image8] is the register count) fail to reliably distinguish ![][image9] from ![][image10] unless ![][image8] is set excessively large. Because distinguishing ![][image9] from ![][image11] is a strict binary threshold required by Q1, HLL is suboptimal for exact low-cardinality classification.

#### **Combinatorial Group Testing (CGT) and Compressed Sensing**

Instead of running ![][image12] individual tests sequentially, CGT runs ![][image13] pooled test batches (![][image14]). Each batch executes a deterministic subset of tests without probe resets between tests within the same batch. The coverage vector of length ![][image15] (where ![][image15] is the total probe count) is recorded once per batch, yielding an ![][image16] dynamic boolean matrix ![][image17]. Given a known ![][image18] test-assignment matrix ![][image19], the system solves ![][image20] for each probe ![][image3], where ![][image21] represents the indicator vector of tests covering probe ![][image3].  
For a probe with multiplicity at most ![][image1], non-adaptive ![][image1]\-disjunct or ![][image1]\-separable measurement matrices guarantee exact identification of ![][image22] with run-count bounds of:

#### **Sparsity Failure Modes in Real Java Codebases**

The fundamental flaw of applying CGT or compressed sensing to JVM code coverage is the breakdown of the sparsity assumption (![][image24]). In real-world enterprise Java systems, probe multiplicities fall into a highly skewed bimodal distribution:

* **Domain Logic Probes:** Highly sparse (![][image25]). CGT reconstructs these probes efficiently with ![][image14].  
* **Infrastructure and Utility Probes:** Non-sparse (![][image26]). Probes located in logging frameworks, string manipulation utilities, base exception handlers, dependency injection containers (e.g., Spring or Guice lifecycle management), and data structure collections are executed by nearly 100% of the test suite.

When ![][image26], ![][image1]\-disjunct matrix requirements dictate that ![][image27]. Under these conditions, decoding algorithms fail, and the execution cost of running ![][image13] pooled runs exceeds ![][image12] individual test runs due to the computational overhead of decoding ![][image15] system equations. Consequently, CGT cannot be relied upon as a primary execution model for general Java codebases.

### **A2. Ablation / Leave-One-Out Mechanics**

Ablation measures attribution causally: to determine if test ![][image2] covers changed line ![][image28], the test engine executes the suite with ![][image2] omitted and measures whether line ![][image28] remains covered in the cumulative coverage report.

#### **Subsetting Algorithms and Cost Profile**

Naive leave-one-out ablation requires executing ![][image12] separate runs of ![][image29] tests, resulting in a total execution time of ![][image30], which is computationally intractable. To optimize this:

* **Binary Search / Delta Debugging (DDmax):** Partition test suite ![][image31] into subsets ![][image32]. If ![][image28] is covered by ![][image31], check if ![][image28] is covered by ![][image33]. If true, ![][image34] contains no unique covers for ![][image28].  
* **Adaptive Group Ablation:** Group tests using static call-graph clusters and ablate entire test packages simultaneously.

#### **Wall-Clock Cost Profile Comparison**

Assuming ![][image35] is the time required to execute the full test suite in parallel (![][image36] for 5,000 tests, modeled under analytical assumptions), the comparative wall-clock costs are detailed in the table below:

| Ablation Strategy | Required Suite Runs | Wall-Clock Cost (Tsuite​=60s,N=5000) | Correctness / Corruption Risk |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Naive Leave-One-Out** | **![][image37]** | **![][image38]** (\~83.3 hours, modeled) | High susceptibility to state leaks |
| **Binary Subsetting (DDmax)** | **![][image39]** | **![][image40]** (\~2.1 hours, modeled) | Flakiness due to missing setup tests |
| **Adaptive Package Ablation** | **![][image41]** | **![][image42]** (\~25 minutes, modeled) | Coarse granularity; misses single-test uniqueness |

#### **Corruption via Test-Order Dependence and Shared State**

Ablation assumes test independence. However, empirical studies show that Java test suites frequently contain order-dependent (OD) and state-polluting tests1. Removing test ![][image43] during ablation can cause a subsequent test ![][image44] to fail or follow an alternate execution path because ![][image43] was responsible for initializing a shared database record, setting a system property, or warming a cache. This corrupts the coverage map, producing both false positives and false negatives for line coverage attribution.

### **A3. Static and Hybrid Attribution Models**

Static attribution constructs a control-flow/call graph from bytecode and identifies which test methods can reach a target line ![][image28]. Hybrid models seed static reachability graphs with dynamic call graph traces obtained from a single cumulative coverage run.

#### **Empirical Precision and Recall in Regression Test Selection (RTS)**

The RTS literature provides benchmark evaluations comparing static tools (e.g., STARTS), dynamic class-level tools (e.g., Ekstazi), and hybrid fine-grained tools (e.g., HyRTS).

| RTS Tool | Granularity | Analysis Paradigm | Precision Violation Rate | Safety / Recall Violation Rate | Average Test Selection Rate |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Ekstazi** \[cite: 3, 4, 5\] | Class Level | Dynamic (Bytecode checksum) | Low (\~15%) | ![][image45] \[cite: 5\] | \~15.95% (84.05% reduction)5 |
| **STARTS** \[cite: 3, 4, 5\] | Class Level | Static (CHA / Call Graph) | Medium (\~31%) | \~5.94% (Reflection, Invokedynamic)5 | \~31.72% (68.28% reduction)5 |
| **HyRTS** \[cite: 4, 5, 6\] | Method / File | Hybrid (Dynamic entry \+ Static method) | Very Low (\~5%) | ![][image45] \[cite: 5, 6\] | \~9% (91% reduction)5 |
| **PKRTS** \[cite: 5\] | Package Level | Static Graph | High (\~62%)5 | \~2.29%5 | \~62.79% (37.21% reduction)5 |

Precision measures the ratio of unneeded tests excluded (higher is better; low precision violation means few unneeded tests selected). Safety/Recall measures whether all tests covering the changed line are correctly identified (low safety violation means critical tests are rarely missed).

#### **Granularity Collapse for Q1 and Q2**

Class-level granularity (used by Ekstazi and STARTS) is sufficient for test selection, but collapses when applied to per-test coverage attribution:

* **Collapse on Q1 (Multiplicity):** If Class ![][image46] contains 10 methods and Test ![][image47] executes C.m1(), while Test ![][image48] executes C.m2(), class-level models report that both ![][image47] and ![][image48] cover Class ![][image46]. For a changed line ![][image28] inside C.m1(), class-level analysis incorrectly reports ![][image10], failing to recognize that ![][image28] is executed exclusively by ![][image47].  
* **Collapse on Q2 (Redundancy):** Two tests executing completely disjoint methods within the same class are marked as 100% overlapping under class-level static graphs, generating severe false-positive redundancy warnings.

Method-level hybrid reachability graphs (e.g., HyRTS) mitigate class-level collapse, but still suffer from imprecise dynamic dispatch resolution (virtual calls resolving to multiple overriding targets) and reflection3.

## **2\. Comparative Analysis of Existing Engines**

### **B1. PITest (pitest.org, Apache-2.0)**

PIT is an open-source mutation testing framework for the JVM that builds an internal test-to-line coverage map during its pre-mutation analysis phase7.

#### **Coverage Collection Architecture**

PIT executes coverage collection inside a dedicated child JVM process (org.pitest.coverage.execute.CoverageMinion)9. The parent process (MutationCoverageReport) spawns JVM minions via command-line invocation and receives dynamic test-to-line maps over TCP sockets9. The minion installs a java.lang.instrument.ClassFileTransformer using ASM9. Bytecode is transformed at load time to insert static callbacks to sun.pitest.CodeCoverageStore9. Global probe arrays are registered per class, and hits are recorded in memory buffers9.  
PIT discovers test units via framework-specific plugins (JUnit 4/5, TestNG) and executes tests sequentially within the minion process11. It communicates with the parent process over a raw TCP socket connection using SafeDataInputStream and SafeDataOutputStream9. Upon completion of each test, probe hits recorded in CodeCoverageStore are transmitted over the socket as line-coverage vectors and reset in memory9.

#### **Data Model Exposure and Machine-Readable Output**

While PIT’s coverage map is primarily internal, it can be exported to disk by setting \<exportLineCoverage\>true\</exportLineCoverage\> in the plugin configuration13. This instructs PIT to write a linecoverage.xml artifact13. The XML format explicitly exposes test-to-line mappings:

XML  
\<coverage\>  
  \<class name\="com.example.OrderService"\>  
    \<method name\="calculateTotal" desc\="(I)V"\>  
      \<line number\="42"\>  
        \<tests\>  
          \<test name\="com.example.OrderServiceTest.testCalculateTotal"/\>  
          \<test name\="com.example.OrderServiceTest.testDiscount"/\>  
        \</tests\>  
      \</line\>  
    \</method\>  
  \</class\>  
\</coverage\>

PIT also exposes a public plugin extension point (org.pitest.coverage.CoverageExporter), introduced in release 1.15.4, allowing custom plugins to inspect the in-memory CoverageData object directly14.

#### **Handling of Attribution Hazards**

PIT manages static initializers through dedicated filtering plugins (+FSTATI / StaticInitializerFilter)15:

* PIT’s static initializer detector identifies code executing within \<clinit\> methods or private static methods invoked exclusively by \<clinit\>18.  
* By default, PIT suppresses mutations inside static initializers because re-transforming class bytecode via the Java Instrumentation API (retransformClasses) does not re-execute \<clinit\> blocks18.  
* **Documented Limitation:** Source code and issue trackers explicitly acknowledge that static initializers are attributed solely to whichever test forces the initial class load18. Subsequent tests relying on the loaded class receive no static initializer coverage attribution18.

#### **Performance Profile**

In benchmark executions, PIT's coverage collection phase (DefaultCoverageGenerator) accounts for approximately 5% to 15% of total mutation testing time8. On a standard suite of 1,000 unit tests, PIT collects line coverage in \~1.2 to 2.8 seconds (measured, source: PIT execution logs)8. This speed is achieved because PIT uses a single child JVM (CoverageMinion) with high-speed in-memory probe array resets and direct socket stream processing8, avoiding external process restarts per test.

### **B2. OpenJDK JCov Test Scales**

JCov is OpenJDK's official code coverage tool, distributed under the GNU General Public License v2 with Classpath Exception (GPLv2+CE)19.

#### **"Test Scales" Architecture and Grabber Protocol**

JCov supports per-test attribution through its **Test Scales** feature19. The system uses a centralized daemon process called the Grabber20:

> 1. The Grabber daemon is initialized with a structural template generated by TmplGen:java \-jar jcov.jar Grabber \-v \-t template.xml start  
>    \[cite: 20\]  
> 2. Tests are executed with the JCov agent attached in grabber mode:-javaagent:jcov.jar=grabber  
>    \[cite: 20\]  
> 3. The test runner passes test boundary signals to the agent via system property updates or socket commands:-Djcov.testname=com.example.MyTest  
>    \[cite: 20\]  
> 4. The agent flushes active probe vectors to the Grabber over socket connections at each test boundary20.

#### **Data Model and Scaling**

JCov models coverage as a dense bit-matrix over total probes ![][image15] and total tests ![][image12]:  
![][image49]  
For a project with ![][image50] probes and ![][image51] tests, the raw uncompressed matrix requires ![][image52]. While memory overhead remains manageable for moderate suites, network serialization overhead via the single TCP Grabber daemon creates bottlenecks when test suites are run across highly parallel test runners.

#### **Licensing Implications**

JCov is licensed under GPLv2 \+ Classpath Exception19.

* **External Process Invocation:** An Apache-2.0 CLI tool can execute JCov as an isolated external process (java \-jar jcov.jar ...) via system execution (ProcessBuilder). This constitutes an aggregate distribution model and does not violate Apache-2.0 licensing constraints.  
* **Direct Library Linking:** Bundling jcov.jar inside an Apache-2.0 distribution or dynamically linking JCov classes into the tool’s primary JVM memory space is legally prohibited under GPLv2 rules.

## **3\. Optimizing Sequential Reset Execution**

If sequential probe resets are used, execution overhead and attribution errors can be mitigated through process parallelism, fast snapshot encoding, and pre-loading static initializers.

### **C1. Process-Level Parallelism (Forked Workers)**

Process-level parallelism uses ![][image5] worker JVM processes (![][image53]). Tests are partitioned into ![][image5] disjoint subsets (![][image54]) and assigned to workers. Each worker runs its assigned tests sequentially, executing reset() and getExecutionData() locally per test.

#### **Speedup Mechanics**

Because probe arrays in JaCoCo (boolean\[\]) are process-local, forking ![][image5] JVM processes eliminates cross-thread data races without requiring lock synchronization on global probe arrays. Speedup approaches the theoretical maximum:  
![][image55]  
For 5,000 tests across 8 CPU cores, total execution time drops from \~25 minutes to \~3.5 minutes (modeled under analytical assumptions).

#### **Class-Loading Attribution Errors across Worker Forks**

While process isolation restores speed, it introduces class-loading attribution drift across forks:

* If Class C is used by Test ![][image47] (assigned to Worker 1\) and Test ![][image56] (assigned to Worker 2), both Worker 1 and Worker 2 must load Class C.  
* Consequently, the \<clinit\> block of Class C is executed **twice**—once in Worker 1 and once in Worker 2\.  
* Static initializers are thus attributed to ![][image47] in Worker 1 AND to ![][image56] in Worker 2\.  
* If ![][image47] and ![][image56] were run sequentially in a single JVM, the static initializer would be attributed **only** to ![][image47].

This error is systematic: forking multiplies static initialization coverage across worker boundaries by a factor proportional to class reloading across workers.

### **C2. Snapshot Cost & In-Memory Data Structures**

The native JaCoCo snapshot method getExecutionData(true) iterates through all loaded class execution data, serializing ExecutionData objects containing boolean\[\] arrays. Serializing full class descriptors per test creates significant overhead.

#### **High-Performance Data Structures: Compressed Roaring Bitmaps**

To achieve sub-millisecond per-test snapshots, JaCoCo’s internal boolean\[\] arrays can be mapped directly into an in-memory **Roaring Bitmap** structure (RoaringBitmap).

> 1. **Global Indexing:** Each probe across the codebase is assigned a unique 32-bit integer ID:  
>    ![][image57]  
> 2. **Dirty-Class Tracking:** Instead of scanning all ![][image15] probes at the end of a test, the instrumented bytecode maintains a concurrent queue (ConcurrentLinkedQueue\<ClassData\>) containing only classes modified during the current test execution.  
> 3. **Snapshot Extraction:** Upon test completion, the agent inspects only the dirty classes, appends set bit indices into a RoaringBitmap, and resets those specific boolean\[\] entries to false.

#### **Memory Footprint Comparison (![][image50] probes, ![][image37] tests)**

| Storage Format | Formula / Representation | Uncompressed Size | Compressed Size (N=5000) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **JaCoCo Serialization (.exec)** | Full object graph per test | \~![][image58] (measured, user setup) | \~![][image59] (modeled) |
| **Dense Boolean BitMatrix** | **![][image60]** | **![][image61]** (modeled) | ![][image61] (modeled) |
| **Sparse Roaring Bitmap** | Compressed run-length / array containers | \~![][image62] (modeled) | **\~![][image63]** (modeled) |

Roaring Bitmaps reduce in-memory snapshot storage by **99.8%**, eliminating garbage collection pressure and disk I/O bottlenecks.

### **C3. Semantics of Load-Time Coverage**

Static initializers (\<clinit\>) and field initializers present a fundamental challenge to code coverage attribution because they run exactly once per class loader instance.

#### **Taxonomy of Attribution Policies**

> 1. **First-Toucher Policy:** Attributes \<clinit\> coverage exclusively to the first test that triggers class loading.  
   * *Tool Usage:* Default behavior of JaCoCo and unconfigured PIT18.  
   * *Defensibility:* Poor. First-toucher attribution is non-deterministic and depends heavily on test execution order.  
> 2. **Ambient / Baseline Bucket Policy:** Class loading is forced prior to running tests, or initial class loading hits are stored in a dedicated system setup bucket.  
   * *Tool Usage:* JCov (when using pre-generated templates)20, Teamscale profiler.  
   * *Defensibility:* High. Excludes static initialization noise from test execution fingerprints, ensuring pure runtime attribution for Q1 and Q2.  
> 3. **All-Dependents Union Policy:** Any test that invokes any method on Class C is artificially credited with the static initializer coverage of Class C.  
   * *Tool Usage:* Static post-processing tools.  
   * *Defensibility:* Medium. Over-attributes coverage, but correctly reflects the logical dependence of tests on class initialization.

#### **Why Delta-of-Cumulative Fails Q1 and Q2**

The tool would conclude that ![][image48] executed zero production lines, missing the 100% redundancy relationship between ![][image47] and ![][image48].

Delta-of-cumulative coverage measures **first-toucher coverage**, not per-test execution coverage.

## **4\. Empirical Validation Design**

### **D1. Falsifiable Fingerprint Stability Metrics**

To decide whether a per-test coverage fingerprinting implementation is deterministic and reliable enough to ship in CI, fingerprint stability must be measured empirically using similarity metrics.

#### **The Jaccard Stability Metric**

Let ![][image80] be the set of covered probe IDs recorded for test ![][image2] during run ![][image81]. The stability between two execution runs ![][image81] and ![][image82] for test ![][image2] is defined by the Jaccard similarity coefficient:  
![][image83]

#### **Experimental Validation Gates**

> 1. **Experiment 1: Repeated Execution (Same Order, Same JVM)**  
   * *Threshold Gate:* Mean Jaccard ![][image84] across all tests.  
   * *Objective:* Confirms deterministic probe recording and absence of random async thread contamination.  
> 2. **Experiment 2: Shuffled Execution (Randomized Test Order)**  
   * *Threshold Gate:* Mean Jaccard ![][image85] (excluding static initializers).  
   * *Objective:* Detects state leaks, class-loading pollution, and order-dependent execution paths.  
> 3. **Experiment 3: Concurrency Isolation (Sequential vs. Forked Parallel)**  
   * *Threshold Gate:* Mean Jaccard ![][image86].  
   * *Objective:* Ensures parallel worker forks do not distort probe attribution compared to single-threaded execution.

An implementation is marked as **PASSED** if and only if all three validation gates are satisfied on a benchmark evaluation suite.

### **D2. Test-Order Dependence and Flakiness Impact**

Test-order dependence directly distorts code coverage fingerprints. When test execution order changes, order-dependent tests alter their execution paths.

#### **Empirical Prevalence in Real-World Java Suites**

Empirical studies using test-reordering frameworks such as **NonDex** and **iDFlakies** provide clear statistics on the prevalence of order-dependent tests in Java open-source projects:

* **iDFlakies Dataset Findings:** In a study of flaky tests across Maven-based Java projects, iDFlakies identified that **50.5% of all flaky tests are order-dependent (OD)**, while 49.5% are non-order-dependent (NOD) (measured, source: iDFlakies study)2.  
* **Types of Order-Dependent Flakies:**  
  * *Victim tests:* Fail or follow alternate branches when run after a specific *Polluter* test.  
  * *Brittle tests:* Pass or execute expected paths only when run after a specific *State-Setter* test.

#### **Implications for Per-Test Attribution**

Because 50.5% of flaky tests alter their execution behavior based on preceding tests2, their probe coverage sets ![][image87] fluctuate under different test runner configurations. If a coverage tool detects a Jaccard stability index ![][image88] for a test under randomized reordering, the tool must flag the test as **Order-Dependent / Flaky** and exclude its fingerprint from redundancy determinations (Q2).

### **D3. False-Positive Risk in Redundancy Detection**

Line-coverage overlap is a **necessary but insufficient** condition for test redundancy. Declaring two tests redundant simply because ![][image89] leads to false positives1.

#### **Causes of False-Positive Redundancy**

> 1. **Assertion Diversity:** ![][image47] and ![][image48] execute the same production path, but ![][image47] asserts boundary conditions on the return value while ![][image48] asserts exception types or state mutations1.  
> 2. **Parameterized / Equivalence Partitioning:** ![][image47] passes positive integers and ![][image48] passes negative integers to method abs(x). Both execute line 10, but they validate distinct domain constraints.

#### **Required Multi-Stage Validation Pipeline**

> 1. **Stage 1: Line-Coverage Overlap Analysis**  
   * Computes Jaccard Similarity ![][image90].  
   * *Filter:* If ![][image91], tests are NOT redundant.  
> 2. **Stage 2: Assertion AST Static Analysis**  
   * Inspects test source ASTs for identical assertion structures.  
   * *Filter:* If ASTs differ, downgrade finding to "Path Overlap, Distinct Assertion Oracles".  
> 3. **Stage 3: Dynamic Mutation Scoring Verification**  
   * Injects mutants into covered production lines.  
   * *Filter:* If ![][image47] kills Mutant ![][image92] but ![][image48] does not kill ![][image92], tests are NOT redundant.

A redundancy finding must only be presented to a developer when all three stages confirm structural, coverage, and assertion identity.

To select the optimal design for a diff-scoped, local CLI tool (operating under Apache-2.0 / BSD constraints), candidate approaches are evaluated using the utility metric:

| **2\. Delta-of-Cumulative Snapshots** | 1 (Fails Q1 and Q2 mathematically) | 10 (Trivial implementation) | 2 (Fast single pass, modeled) | **5.0** | **REJECTED:** Mathematically invalid for Q1/Q2. |

| **4\. Hybrid Static Call Graph (HyRTS style)** | 6 (Misses dynamic dispatch/reflection)3 | 5 (Requires bytecode analyzer) | 1 (Extremely fast static pass, modeled) | **30.0** | **REJECTED:** Insufficient granularity for Q1/Q2. |
| **5\. Forked Parallel Worker Pool \+ In-Memory Roaring Bitmaps** | 9 (High precision; handles isolation) | 7 (Custom Agent \+ JUnit Listener) | 2 (Fast: \~![][image94] mins parallel, modeled) | **31.5** | **RECOMMENDED (Primary Engine)** |
| **6\. PITest Coverage Minion Engine Integration** | 9 (Proven industrial line map)8 | 8 (Leverages Apache-2.0 PIT core)7 | 3 (Optimized IPC socket stream, measured)8 | **24.0** | **RECOMMENDED (Alternative Option)** |

### **Defended Architectural Recommendation**

For a deterministic, local CLI tool operating pre-push, the recommended architecture combines **Forked Process Parallelism (Candidate 5\)** with a **Custom ASM Bytecode Agent and In-Memory Roaring Bitmap Storage**:

> 1. **Pre-Suite Forced Class Pre-Loading:** Before test execution, the CLI tool reflectively loads all project classes using Class.forName(). This moves \<clinit\> static initializers into a baseline setup bucket, isolating per-test fingerprints from class-loader noise.  
> 2. **Forked Parallel Execution Worker Pool:** The tool forks ![][image5] worker JVM processes (![][image53]). Tests are assigned across workers in class-level batches to minimize process overhead.  
> 3. **Dirty-Class Bitmap Tracking:** The custom Java agent instruments bytecode to track dirty classes in a concurrent queue. At test boundaries, the agent flushes modified probe IDs directly into an in-memory RoaringBitmap, clearing only the dirty entries.  
> 4. **Validation and Verdict Filtering:** Coverage fingerprints are evaluated against Jaccard stability metrics. Any detected test redundancy (Q2) is passed through an AST assertion analyzer before emitting a finding to the developer.

This approach eliminates the performance bottlenecks of naive resets, satisfies Apache-2.0 licensing constraints, and provides accurate per-test coverage attribution for modified code diffs.
